evidence: src/infrastructure/server.ts: the only export is `createServer(repository: Repository): express.Application`; it builds `new TaskService(repository)` and sends every route through it (createProject, createUser, addTask, assignTask, markTaskDone, listTasks).
src/infrastructure/server.ts: errors are handled in one place, the final `app.use((error, req, res, next) => res.status(400)...)` middleware, and every handler calls `next(error)`.

src/infrastructure/server.ts: the same `if (!id || !name) { res.status(400).json({ error: 'Missing id or name' }) }` check appears in both POST /projects and POST /users. This is minor duplication of request-shape validation, not of a domain invariant.
src/infrastructure/server.ts: GET /projects/:projectId/tasks uses `status: status as any`, which skips type checking for the filter but still calls taskService.listTasks.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: The unit has one file, src/infrastructure/server.ts, and it covers a single concern: the HTTP adapter. Its one export, createServer, builds an Express app and connects each route to a TaskService method. Every handler follows the same pattern: read the request, do a basic presence check, call TaskService, send JSON, and pass errors to next(). One shared error middleware handles all errors. No handler calls the Repository directly or adds domain logic, so the module consistently uses TaskService. Two small weaknesses are not enough to fail it. First, the POST /projects and POST /users handlers repeat the same check ('Missing id or name'). This is basic request-shape validation for two different resources, not a duplicated domain invariant. Second, the GET tasks handler uses `status as any`, which skips type checking for the status filter. It is a typing shortcut, but the request still goes through TaskService.listTasks, so the module's own abstraction is not bypassed. Import direction is out of scope for this review.
